title: Beige Book — June 4, 2025
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2025-06-04 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Activity declined slightly. Half the Districts (six) reported slight to moderate declines, three no change and three slight growth. The report cited "elevated levels of economic and policy uncertainty" in all Districts, making businesses and households hesitant. Manufacturing declined slightly. Residential sales were little changed, and new home construction was flat or slowing in most reports. Loan demand and capital spending plans were mixed. Port activity was robust, while transportation and warehousing elsewhere were mixed. The outlook stayed slightly pessimistic and uncertain. The report was prepared by the St. Louis Fed.

Consumer spending

Mixed, with most Districts reporting slight declines or no change. Some Districts saw higher spending on goods expected to be hit by tariffs.

Labor markets

Employment was little changed: most Districts flat, three slight-to-modest gains, two slight declines. All Districts described lower labor demand—fewer hours and overtime, hiring pauses and staff-reduction plans. Some sectors had layoffs, but they were not widespread. Turnover fell and applicant pools grew. Wage growth was modest, with many Districts reporting easing pressure, though a few said higher living costs still pushed wages up.

Prices

Prices rose moderately, and contacts widely expected faster increases ahead; a few called expected cost increases strong or substantial. Every District reported tariffs pushing up costs and prices. Firms responded by raising prices on affected or all items, absorbing costs through thinner margins, or adding surcharges. Firms planning to pass tariff costs along expected to do so within three months.

Notable themes

  • Tariffs: Raising costs in all twelve Districts; pre-tariff buying lifted some goods spending and port volumes.
  • Uncertainty: Elevated everywhere, delaying hiring and investment.
  • Labor demand cooling: Universal reports of softer demand, but few layoffs.

District highlights

  • Boston: Slight decline; hiring paused; larger summer price increases expected.
  • New York: Modest decline; strong tariff-driven input cost growth vs. moderate selling-price increases; outlook quite pessimistic.
  • Philadelphia: Second straight modest decline.
  • Cleveland: Tariffs drove sharp cost increases.
  • Richmond: Port volumes rose strongly on an import surge.
  • Chicago: Slight growth; 2025 farm income prospects improved somewhat.
  • Minneapolis: Some employers prepared layoff contingency plans; tariff surcharges added or considered.
  • Kansas City: Moderate decline on weaker retail and single-family housing demand.
  • Dallas: Outlooks worsened; tariff uncertainty made planning difficult.

Read-through for SPY

  • The first outright (slight) decline of the year signaled a cooling economy, a risk to earnings growth.
  • Expected tariff pass-through within three months pointed to a summer inflation bump that could delay Fed easing.
  • Softer labor demand without widespread layoffs suggested a slowdown, not a collapse, as of this report.
